content:
Yes, you can combine aggregate functions with CASE expressions. Here’s an example:
```sql
SELECT
  SUM(total_amount) AS total_sales,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN total_amount > 100 THEN 1 END) AS high_value_orders
FROM orders;
```
Oh, I didn’t know I could put a CASE inside COUNT like that.
Yep! CASE is really versatile. You can use it anywhere you’d use a column expression.
Can I also calculate how many were below $50, and how many in between?

Absolutely. Just expand the CASE blocks:
```sql
SELECT
  COUNT(CASE WHEN total_amount < 50 THEN 1 END) AS low_orders,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN total_amount BETWEEN 50 AND 100 THEN 1 END) AS medium_orders,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN total_amount > 100 THEN 1 END) AS high_orders
FROM orders;
```
Wow, that’s super readable. Can I label each row with its order category too?

You can do that row-wise like this:
```sql
SELECT
  order_id,
  total_amount,
  CASE
    WHEN total_amount > 100 THEN 'High'
    WHEN total_amount >= 50 THEN 'Medium'
    ELSE 'Low'
  END AS category
FROM orders;
```
Nice! And if I want totals per category?

Just use a GROUP BY on that CASE:
```sql
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN total_amount > 100 THEN 'High'
    WHEN total_amount >= 50 THEN 'Medium'
    ELSE 'Low'
  END AS category,
  COUNT(*) AS num_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY category;
```
Thank you! This really clears things up.
